state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think the range wouldn't change if all the plants were cut in half or grew by the same amount? Can you think of a counterexample where changing all values by the same proportion would actually affect the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess I thought that if you just change all the numbers by the same amount, it wouldn't really matter for the range. But now I'm not sure. Could you explain how the range changes if you add or multiply all the heights? Like, what exactly happens to the highest and lowest values?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a situation where changing all the heights by the same amount would actually affect the range? How would changing all the heights by a certain factor impact the highest and lowest values in the set?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly asks vague questions without addressing the specific misconception, fails to distinguish between additive and multiplicative changes (domain error), and the student shows no improvement—ending more confused than at the start.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking and never directly provides answers, though they could have more effectively used a concrete counterexample to expose the student's flawed reasoning about multiplication versus addition.
